title: Freelance Year-End Review Kit
description: Close out the year and plan the next one in one afternoon. A 30-item December admin checklist, a month-by-month income and hours tracker, a client review sheet that shows your real hourly rate per client, 20 guided review questions, a keep / raise / reshape / release method with ready-to-send emails, and a next-year plan that works out your monthly target from your own costs. Every file has a worked example. For freelancers and solo businesses.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Year-End Review Kit

Most freelancers end the year with a vague feeling: "it was busy" or "it was slow". This kit turns that feeling into numbers and decisions in one focused afternoon (about three hours), so you go into next year knowing which clients to keep, which to raise, which work to drop and what you need to earn each month.

It works for any freelancer or solo business: designers, developers, writers, editors, consultants, photographers, virtual assistants.

## The review in five steps

| Step | Time | File | What you end up with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Tidy up the year | 45 min | `december-checklist.md` | Invoices chased, receipts gathered, files backed up |
| 2. Your year in numbers | 45 min | `year-in-numbers.csv` | Monthly income, hours and effective hourly rate |
| 3. Review every client | 30 min | `client-review.csv` | Revenue, effective rate and a score for each client |
| 4. Decide what changes | 30 min | `client-decisions.md` + `year-end-review.md` | Keep, raise, reshape or release for each client; your lessons |
| 5. Plan next year | 30 min | `next-year-plan.md` | A monthly income target, a capacity check and three priorities |

Do the steps in order. Step 4 depends on the numbers from steps 2 and 3, and the plan in step 5 depends on the decisions in step 4.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `december-checklist.md` | 30-item admin checklist for closing out the year |
| `year-in-numbers.csv` | Month-by-month tracker with a filled example year |
| `client-review.csv` | One row per client: revenue, hours, effective rate, scores |
| `year-end-review.md` | 20 guided questions, with a filled example answer for each section |
| `client-decisions.md` | The keep / raise / reshape / release method, with example emails |
| `next-year-plan.md` | Work out your monthly target from your real costs, check it fits your hours, set priorities |

## How to use the spreadsheets

Open the `.csv` files in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers. Each has a worked example (a fictional freelance designer, "Sam") so you can see what good entries look like. Delete the example rows, or keep them to compare, and add your own.

Two numbers matter most:

- **Effective hourly rate** = money received ÷ all hours spent (including emails, calls, revisions and admin for that client). This is what you really earned per hour, not what you quoted.
- **Share of income** = one client's revenue ÷ your total revenue. If one client is more than about 40% of your income, losing them would hurt badly; that's worth knowing.

## A note on money

This kit helps you look at your own numbers and set your own targets. It isn't tax, accounting or financial advice. For tax deadlines, what you can deduct, and how much to set aside, ask an accountant or your local tax authority, and bring the summary from `year-in-numbers.csv` with you: it'll make that conversation shorter.

## When to do it

Any time in the last six weeks of the year or the first two weeks of the next. Block the time in your calendar like client work. If you can't find three hours, do steps 1 and 3 now: they have the most impact.
files.client-decisions.md:
# Keep, Raise, Reshape or Release

Every client gets one of four decisions. Use the scores in `client-review.csv` as your starting point, then use your judgement: the numbers inform the decision, they don't make it.

## The four decisions

| Decision | When it fits | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep** | Good rate, easy to work with, work you like (total score 13 or more and effective rate at or above your average) | Thank them, and ask about next year's plans |
| **Raise** | Good client, but the effective rate is below your average or below your current price | Give notice of a new rate, with a start date 6 to 12 weeks away |
| **Reshape** | The client is worth keeping but the way you work together isn't working (scope creep, slow payment, chaotic briefs) | Change the terms: fixed price, deposits, revision limits, payment terms |
| **Release** | Low rate, low scores, and fixing it would take more effort than replacing the income | Finish current work well, then step back politely and, where you can, refer them on |

## A quick decision path

1. **Is the effective rate at or above your yearly average?**
   - Yes: go to 2.
   - No: go to 3.
2. **Is the total score 13 or more?**
   - Yes: **Keep.**
   - No: **Reshape** (good money, bad process: fix the process).
3. **Is the total score 13 or more?**
   - Yes: **Raise** (good relationship, too cheap: fix the price).
   - No: go to 4.
4. **Is this client more than 15% of your income, or a strong source of referrals?**
   - Yes: **Reshape** first, and reconsider in six months.
   - No: **Release.**

The path is a starting point. Override it when you know something the numbers don't, such as a client who's about to sign a big project, or one you simply don't want to work with.

## Before you release a client, check your safety margin

Releasing a client is easier if the income gap is small or already covered. Ask:

- How many months of essential costs could I cover from savings if this income stopped?
- Is new work already in the pipeline that would replace it?
- Could I release them in three months instead of now, while I find a replacement?

If the answers are uncomfortable, choose **Reshape** for now and set a date to look again.

---

## Example emails

Replace everything in [brackets]. Send each in its own email, not tucked into a project update.

### Keep: "What's coming next year?"

> Subject: Plans for [next year]?
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thanks for a great year. [The spring packaging] was one of my favourite projects, and I loved seeing [it in shops].
>
> I'm planning my schedule for [next year] now. Do you have anything coming up that you'd like help with? If you let me know roughly when, I'll keep space for it.
>
> [your name]

### Raise: rate notice

> Subject: My rates from [date]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I've really enjoyed working on [the clinic website] this year, and I'd love to keep going.
>
> I'm updating my rates for [next year]. From [date, 6 to 12 weeks away], the monthly retainer will be [new amount] (currently [old amount]). Everything else stays the same: [the same hours, response times and monthly report].
>
> Anything booked before [date] stays at the current rate. If you'd like to talk about it, I'm happy to jump on a call.
>
> [your name]

### Reshape: new terms

> Subject: A small change to how we work on [decks]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Looking back at this year's projects, I've noticed [decks often grow after the brief], which makes timing and cost hard to predict for both of us.
>
> From [date], I'd like to quote each [deck] at a fixed price, with [two] rounds of revisions included and anything new quoted separately before I start. I'll also ask for [50%] up front on projects over [amount].
>
> I think this will make budgeting simpler on your side too. Happy to talk it through.
>
> [your name]

### Release: stepping back

> Subject: My availability from [date]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Thank you for the work this year. I'm narrowing my focus to [brand and packaging projects] next year, so after [the current batch, finishing on date] I won't be taking on new [social media work].
>
> I'll make sure everything is finished and handed over properly, with all files in [shared folder]. If it helps, I can recommend [a designer who specialises in this / a couple of people] to take it on.
>
> It's been good working with you, and I wish you all the best.
>
> [your name]

## Common mistakes

- **Raising rates with no notice.** Give at least six weeks, more for retainers.
- **Releasing a client by going quiet.** Always finish and hand over properly. Your reputation travels further than any one client.
- **Reshaping in the middle of a project.** New terms start with the next project or the next billing period.
- **Deciding everything at once.** If you have more than two Raise or Release decisions, space them out over a few months so your income doesn't drop all at once.

files.december-checklist.md:
# December Close-Out Checklist

Work through this before the holidays. Tick each item or write "n/a". Most items take under five minutes; the whole list takes about 45 minutes, plus waiting time for replies.

## Money in

- [ ] List every unpaid invoice, with its amount and due date
- [ ] Send a polite reminder for anything overdue (see the template below)
- [ ] Invoice any finished work you haven't billed yet, including small extras and expenses
- [ ] Check which clients close their books or freeze payments over the holidays, and invoice them before that date
- [ ] Note any client who paid late more than once this year (you'll use this in `client-review.csv`)
- [ ] Confirm deposits for any project starting in January

## Money out

- [ ] List every software subscription you pay for, with its monthly or yearly cost
- [ ] Cancel anything you didn't use in the last three months
- [ ] Note which subscriptions renew in January, and decide now whether to keep them
- [ ] Gather all receipts for business expenses into one folder, named by month
- [ ] Download statements for any business bank account and card for the full year

## Records

- [ ] Export your invoices for the year (from your invoicing tool or spreadsheet) into one file
- [ ] Export your time-tracking data for the year, if you track time
- [ ] Fill in `year-in-numbers.csv` from these exports
- [ ] Write down any questions for your accountant as you go (keep a list at the bottom of this file)
- [ ] Check when your tax filing and payment deadlines are, and add them to your calendar

## Clients and work

- [ ] Send each active client your holiday availability (dates off, when you reply, who to contact if urgent)
- [ ] Ask happy clients from this year whether they have work planned for the first quarter
- [ ] Ask two or three happy clients for a short written testimonial while the work is fresh (use their real words; never write it for them)
- [ ] Add finished projects to your portfolio, or at least save the files and a one-line note about the result
- [ ] Archive finished projects: final files, contract, invoices and key emails in one folder each

## Your setup

- [ ] Back up your work computer and check the backup actually opens
- [ ] Update passwords for your email, bank and any tool that holds client data
- [ ] Turn on two-factor sign-in anywhere it's still off
- [ ] Clear your desktop and downloads folder (archive, don't delete, if unsure)
- [ ] Check your website and profiles show your current services and prices

## You

- [ ] Book your days off for next year now: holidays first, then work fits around them
- [ ] Write down the three best moments of the year (you'll use them in `year-end-review.md`)
- [ ] Write down the three worst (same)
- [ ] Block three hours for the rest of this kit

---

## Payment reminder template

> Subject: Invoice [number] before the holidays
>
> Hi [name],
>
> A quick one before everyone logs off for the year: invoice [number] for [project], [amount], was due on [date]. I've attached it again in case it got buried.
>
> If it's already on its way, thank you, and please ignore this. If anything's holding it up, let me know and I'll help sort it out.
>
> Wishing you a good break,
> [your name]

## Holiday availability template

> Subject: My holiday schedule
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I'm taking a break from [date] to [date] and will be back on [date]. Anything you send in that time will be answered then.
>
> If you'd like anything finished before the break, please send it by [date] so I can fit it in.
>
> Thanks for a great year working together.
> [your name]

files.next-year-plan.md:
# Next Year Plan

This page turns your review into three things: a monthly income target based on your real costs, a check that the target fits the hours you actually want to work, and three priorities. Fill in the right-hand column with your own numbers. Sam's example is beside it.

All amounts are before tax unless you choose otherwise. How much to set aside for tax depends on where you live and your situation; ask an accountant or your tax authority and put their figure in line C.

## Part 1: What do I need to earn?

| Line | Item | Sam | You |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | What I want to pay myself for the year (personal living costs, savings, extras) | $42,000 | |
| B | Business costs for the year (software, equipment, insurance, accountant, training). Use last year's total from `year-in-numbers.csv` and adjust | $3,200 | |
| C | Tax and contributions set aside (the figure from your accountant or tax authority) | $13,000 | |
| D | Buffer for slow months and late payers (we suggest 10% of A + B + C) | $5,800 | |
| E | **Yearly income target** (A + B + C + D) | **$64,000** | |
| F | Months I'll work (12 minus the months of time off) | 11 | |
| G | **Monthly income target** (E ÷ F) | **$5,818** | |

Compare G with last year: Sam received $60,100 over 12 months, about $5,000 a month. The new target needs about 16% more per working month, with a month more time off. That's a stretch, but the rate and client decisions below cover most of it.

## Part 2: Does it fit my hours?

| Line | Item | Sam | You |
|---|---|---|---|
| H | Weeks I'll work (52 minus holidays, public holidays and a few sick days) | 45 | |
| I | Hours a week I want to work in total | 30 | |
| J | Total hours available (H × I) | 1,350 | |
| K | Share of time on admin and marketing (last year: admin hours ÷ total hours from `year-in-numbers.csv`) | 18% | |
| L | Hours available for client work (J × (1 − K)) | 1,107 | |
| M | **Rate I need per client hour** (E ÷ L) | **$57.81** | |
| N | Effective rate I achieved last year (total received ÷ client hours) | $70.37 | |

**How to read it:**

- If **N is comfortably above M**, the target fits. Your challenge is finding enough work, not price.
- If **N is close to or below M**, you need some combination of higher prices, fewer unpaid hours, less admin, or more hours. Pick one lever at a time.
- If **M is far above anything you've charged**, revisit lines A, D or I. A plan you won't hit isn't a plan.

> Sam's N ($70.37) is above M ($57.81), so the target fits if Sam can keep the same amount of client work while taking more time off. Sam also wants to cut admin from 18% to 15% by sending invoices on delivery and using proposal templates.

Note the difference between N here and the "effective hourly rate" in `year-in-numbers.csv`. The spreadsheet divides by *all* hours (client plus admin) to show what your time is really worth. Line N divides by *client* hours only, so it can be compared with line M, which already sets aside admin time in line K.

## Part 3: Where will the money come from?

List your expected income sources for the year. Be realistic: only count repeat work if the client has said so.

| Source | Type | Expected for the year | How sure (high / medium / low) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Harbor Bakery | Repeat brand and packaging | $15,000 | Medium: spring range discussed |
| Northfield Clinic | Retainer after 15% increase | $13,500 | High: retainer runs to December |
| Pine & Co Agency | Subcontract | $11,000 | Medium |
| Atlas Logistics | Fixed-price decks | $6,000 | Low: depends on new terms |
| New brand and packaging clients | Referrals and portfolio | $18,500 | Low: needs active marketing |
| **Total** | | **$64,000** | |

Add up only the **high** and **medium** rows. That's your safe base (Sam: $39,500). The gap between the safe base and your target is what your marketing needs to win (Sam: $24,500, roughly four new brand projects).

## Part 4: Three priorities

Pick three. Not ten. Each one gets a first step and a date in the next 30 days.

| # | Priority | Why it matters | First step | By when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |
| 3 | | | | |

> **Sam's priorities:**
> 1. More brand and packaging work: add the Harbor case study to the portfolio, and email five past clients by 15 January.
> 2. Fix the Atlas relationship or replace it: propose fixed-price decks by 10 January.
> 3. Take 25 days off: book all holidays in the calendar by 31 December.

## Part 5: Check in every quarter

Put four 30-minute appointments in your calendar now: early April, July, October and next December. At each one:

1. Compare money received so far with G × months worked so far.
2. Re-score any client who changed.
3. Check the three priorities: done, on track, or dropped?
4. Adjust the plan. A plan that changes is fine; a plan you never look at again isn't.
files.year-end-review.md:
# Year-End Review: 20 Questions

Answer these after you've filled in `year-in-numbers.csv` and `client-review.csv`. Write short, honest answers: bullet points are fine. Each section has an example answer from "Sam", the fictional designer in the spreadsheets, so you can see the level of detail that's useful.

Set a timer for 45 minutes. If you get stuck on one question, skip it and come back.

---

## 1. Money (look at `year-in-numbers.csv`)

1. What did I actually receive this year, and how does it compare with what I expected?
2. What was my effective hourly rate across the whole year?
3. Which were my best and worst months for money received, and why?
4. How many hours went on admin and unpaid work (proposals, email, invoicing, marketing)? Is that more or less than I'd guess?
5. How long did clients take to pay, on average? Who was slowest?

> **Sam's answers:** Received $60,100, about $5,000 more than I expected. Effective rate $57.40, lower than my quoted $75, mostly because of admin (193 hours, nearly a fifth of all my time) and one difficult client. Best month for money in was October (catching up on September's work); worst was August, when I spent 22 hours on proposals that didn't land. Most clients paid within 30 days; Riverside Gym and Atlas took 45 to 60.

## 2. Clients (look at `client-review.csv`)

6. Which client was the best to work with, and what made them good?
7. Which client cost me the most time or energy for the money?
8. Does any single client make up more than about 40% of my income?
9. Where did my new clients come from (referral, website, platform, cold outreach, past client)?
10. Which client would I most like more work from, and have I told them?

> **Sam's answers:** Harbor Bakery: clear briefs, quick decisions, paid on time, and the work is in my portfolio. Atlas Logistics took 205 hours for $9,800 because decks kept growing. No client above 25%, which is good. Five of eight new clients came from referrals (two from Harbor). I want more from Harbor and haven't asked directly.

## 3. Work

11. Which project am I proudest of, and why?
12. Which type of work did I enjoy most? Which did I dread?
13. Which type of work earned the highest effective rate?
14. What did I keep doing for free that I should charge for?
15. Which skill grew most this year, and which do I want to grow next?

> **Sam's answers:** Proudest: Harbor's packaging, it's on shelves and they sold out the first run. Most enjoyed: packaging and brand work; dreaded: social media graphics. Highest rate: agency subcontracting ($82/hour), because the briefs arrive finished. Free work: extra revision rounds on decks, and "quick" logo tweaks for past clients. Grew most: packaging print production; next: motion for brand work.

## 4. Me

16. When was I most tired, and what caused it?
17. How many real days off did I take? Was it enough?
18. What one habit or system helped most this year?
19. What one thing would I stop doing if I could?

> **Sam's answers:** June and September: too many projects overlapping and saying yes to rush jobs. Took 15 working days off; not enough, I want 25. Best system: sending invoices on the day of delivery. Stop: taking on small social media work.

## 5. One sentence

20. If next year goes well, what will be different by this time next year?

> **Sam's answer:** I'll earn about the same from fewer, bigger brand and packaging projects, and take five weeks off.

---

## Turn answers into actions

Read your answers back and pick out anything that's a decision. Write each one below with a date. Keep it to five; anything else goes on a "later" list.

| Decision | First step | By when |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

> **Sam's list:** Raise Northfield's retainer by 15% (send the email by 10 Dec). Change Atlas to fixed-price decks with two rounds (propose in January). Stop taking social media work (refer Riverside on). Ask Harbor about the spring range. Book 25 days off before January.
